results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The closest direct match is Kevin Rajan’s Evolve, but the broader open-source landscape splits into SDLC-specific systems, orchestration runtimes, and evidence/evaluation tooling.

Top recommendations

1. Evolve — autonomous AI SDLC with shipping gates

Kevin Rajan / zer0 ships Evolve, an open-source framework specifically framed around autonomous software development rather than generic agent chat:

- Multi-agent planning, coding, testing, review, and deployment workflows
- Parallel sessions and isolated worktrees
- SPARC-style specification, architecture, TDD, refinement, and completion phases
- C(RAID): research → analysis → integration → deployment → feedback
- Quality gates and deployment validation as part of the workflow

Docs: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/  
Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve  
AI-SDLC tooling hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html

This is the most literal match for “agent orchestration plus evidence-based shipping.” It is especially relevant if you want an opinionated development operating model, not merely an API for agents to message one another.

Related niche components from the same public toolchain:

- tmux-agent-fleet — a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for monitoring Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, and other coding agents across tmux panes: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet
- zer0-pm — deterministic issue graph, ledger, fleet scheduler, and benchmarks: https://github.com/kvnloo/_pm

tmux-agent-fleet is an operations surface rather than an orchestration engine; zer0-pm is closer to the evidence, scheduling, and work-ledger layer.

2. OpenHands — self-hosted coding-agent control plane

OpenHands is one of the most substantial public engineering-agent platforms:

- Runs its own agent plus Claude Code, Codex, and ACP-compatible agents
- Supports local, Docker, VM, remote, and cloud backends
- Provides an Agent Canvas for managing concurrent engineering work
- Includes GitHub, Slack, Linear, webhook, and scheduled automations

Source: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands  
Docs: https://docs.openhands.dev/  
Automation docs: https://docs.openhands.dev/openhands/usage/agent-canvas/prebuilt-automations

Choose OpenHands when you want a self-hostable agent execution platform and developer control plane. It is less opinionated than Evolve about the full evidence-to-ship methodology, so you may need to add your own acceptance gates, artifact ledger, and review policy.

3. Microsoft Agent Framework — production orchestration primitives

Microsoft Agent Framework is Microsoft’s current open-source framework for production-grade agents and multi-agent workflows:

- Sequential, concurrent, handoff, and group-collaboration patterns
- Checkpointing, restartability, streaming, and time travel
- Human-in-the-loop workflow interruption
- OpenTelemetry observability
- Python and .NET support
- Experimental benchmarking packages

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework  
Docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/

It is a strong foundation for building a custom AI-SDLC platform, but it does not supply a complete software-delivery operating model out of the box.

Important: Microsoft AutoGen is now in maintenance mode, and its own repository directs new users to Microsoft Agent Framework:

https://github.com/microsoft/autogen

4. LangGraph — durable graph runtime for custom agent factories

LangGraph is a low-level runtime for long-running, stateful agent workflows:

- Durable execution and recovery
- Explicit graph state and transitions
- Human-in-the-loop interrupts
- Persistent memory
- Subagents through higher-level Deep Agents
- Strong tracing when paired with LangSmith

Source: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph  
Durable execution: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/durable-execution  
Human review/interrupts: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts

It is a good choice when you want to design your own deterministic SDLC graph—plan, implement, test, review, benchmark, approve, merge—but it is infrastructure, not a ready-made autonomous software company.

5. MetaGPT — software-company roles and SOPs

MetaGPT models a software organization using product-manager, architect, project-manager, and engineer roles. Its “Code = SOP(Team)” approach produces requirements, designs, APIs, data structures, documentation, and implementation artifacts.

Source: https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT

This is useful for role-oriented, artifact-producing SDLC experiments. Evaluate generated code and test quality independently; producing many lifecycle documents is not automatically the same as producing verified shipping evidence.

6. CrewAI — approachable role and workflow orchestration

CrewAI offers two useful abstraction levels:

- Crews for autonomous, role-based collaboration
- Flows for explicit event-driven control

Source: https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI  
Docs: https://docs.crewai.com/

It is approachable and flexible, but general-purpose. An evidence-based engineering system still needs repository isolation, CI integration, acceptance criteria, reproducible checks, review checkpoints, and provenance storage layered on top.

7. ChatDev — virtual software company and zero-code orchestration

ChatDev started as a virtual software company with CEO, CTO, programmer, tester, and reviewer agents. ChatDev 2.0 has broadened into a zero-code multi-agent orchestration platform; the original software-development system remains on its legacy branch.

Current source: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev  
Original SDLC implementation: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/chatdev1.0

It remains relevant for research into communicative software-development teams, though the current main branch is no longer narrowly focused on software delivery.

Evidence and evaluation companion

mini-SWE-agent is not itself a multi-agent orchestrator, but it is worth pairing with one because its execution history is intentionally linear and inspectable, and it supports batch inference, trajectory browsing, sandboxed execution, and SWE-bench evaluation.

Source: https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent  
Docs: https://mini-swe-agent.com/latest/  
SWE-bench: https://www.swebench.com/

This is a useful model for what “evidence” should mean: reproducible environment, complete trajectory, generated patch, test result, cost record, and benchmark outcome—not simply an agent saying that a task is complete.

Practical shortlist

- Most direct autonomous AI-SDLC match: Evolve
- Most complete self-hosted coding-agent platform: OpenHands
- Best production orchestration foundation: Microsoft Agent Framework
- Best custom durable workflow runtime: LangGraph
- Best role/SOP-based software-company simulation: MetaGPT
- Best lightweight evidence/evaluation companion: mini-SWE-agent
- Best niche local fleet navigation: tmux-agent-fleet
- Best public issue-graph/ledger component: zer0-pm

For evidence-based shipping, I would judge any framework on whether it produces and preserves:

1. A requirement and explicit acceptance criteria
2. An isolated worktree or sandbox
3. Agent execution trajectories and tool outputs
4. The exact patch or commit under review
5. Test, lint, type-check, security, and benchmark results
6. Reviewer findings and remediation history
7. Human approval where risk requires it
8. A durable issue/PR/release ledger with provenance

Many projects provide multi-agent conversation. Far fewer provide that complete chain from intent to independently inspectable shipping evidence. Evolve, OpenHands plus an evidence layer, or a custom Microsoft Agent Framework/LangGraph pipeline are the strongest starting points for that narrower requirement.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: **tmux-agent-fleet** is exactly that.

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

It is an open-source tmux plugin providing a searchable `fzf` command palette across existing tmux panes:

- Zero daemon: discovers agents from local tmux process metadata.
- Harness-neutral: detects Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Pi, Oh My Pi, Fable, ordinary shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions.
- Non-invasive: does not inject commands, rename panes, manage worktrees, or take ownership of sessions.
- Live preview: inspect a pane before jumping to it.
- Fuzzy filtering: search by harness, project, location, or task title.
- Default shortcut: `prefix + f`.
- Dependencies: tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and `fzf`.

TPM installation:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

Then reload TPM with `prefix + I`.

The main limitation follows directly from being harness-neutral: activity status comes from tmux pane activity rather than vendor-specific states such as “waiting for permission.”

Primary references:

- Project and documentation: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet
- Public agent-orchestration hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html
- tmux: https://github.com/tmux/tmux
- fzf: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan describes code as a means of distributing capability and agency:

> “Code is the great equalizer. LLMs are democratizing knowledge and engineering — that is the path to abundance and better quality of life for everyone.”

By “automating humanitarian causes,” he means applying autonomous systems to areas such as health, infrastructure, and open systems—making useful competence available without traditional gatekeepers. His stated goal is for important actions to become dependable and automatic, requiring little or no conscious coordination, while enabling more people to turn ideas into working software.

In short: code equalizes access to capability; automation makes that capability compound at societal scale.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about 25 minutes; serves 2–3.

### Ingredients

- 225 g (8 oz) pasta
- 225–300 g (8–10 oz) mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups fresh spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tbsp butter
- ¾ cup heavy cream or half-and-half
- ½ cup finely grated Parmesan
- ½ tsp dried thyme or Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: red-pepper flakes, lemon juice, chopped parsley

### Method

1. Cook the pasta in well-salted water until just al dente. Reserve 1 cup pasta water, then drain.
2. Heat the oil and butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a mostly even layer. Cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring only occasionally, until deeply browned.
3. Lower the heat to medium. Add the garlic, seasoning, a pinch of salt, black pepper, and optional pepper flakes. Cook for 30 seconds.
4. Add the cream and simmer gently for 2 minutes.
5. Stir in the spinach until wilted. Add the pasta and Parmesan, then toss until glossy. Loosen with reserved pasta water, a splash at a time.
6. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Finish with a small squeeze of lemon if the sauce tastes too rich.

For a lighter version, replace the cream with ¾ cup pasta water and add an extra tablespoon of butter and Parmesan. For more protein, add white beans, shredded rotisserie chicken, or browned Italian sausage.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
As of July 2026, public tooling falls into three distinct groups: full AI-SDLC systems, coding-agent platforms with reproducible traces, and general orchestration libraries. Few projects genuinely combine orchestration with independently checkable shipping evidence.

## Strongest matches

| Project | What it ships | Evidence model | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| [AI-SDLC Framework](https://github.com/ai-sdlc-framework/ai-sdlc) | Autonomous issue-to-PR pipeline, isolated worktrees, parallel reviewers, policy gates | Signed DSSE attestations, cross-harness reviewer independence, checkpoints, structured quality gates | Closest literal match to “evidence-based shipping.” Promising but currently `v1alpha1`; autonomous orchestration is marked experimental. |
| [metaswarm](https://github.com/dsifry/metaswarm) | 18-role SDLC swarm for Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI; issue-to-merged-PR workflow | Orchestrator reruns validation, adversarial review requires `file:line` evidence, blocking coverage thresholds, CI monitoring, Playwright screenshots | Strongest ready-made multi-agent development methodology. Evidence enforcement is mostly git, scripts, prompts, tests, and review rubrics rather than cryptographic attestations. |
| [Routa](https://github.com/phodal/routa) | Workspace/Kanban-based multi-agent delivery with MCP, ACP, and A2A support | Every card accumulates canonical acceptance criteria, implementation evidence, test results, per-criterion verification, and an independent verdict | Excellent niche option when you want evidence to live with the work item. Particularly clear separation between implementer and verifier. |
| [Open SWE](https://github.com/langchain-ai/open-swe) | Asynchronous internal coding-agent architecture: subagents, sandboxes, Slack/Linear/GitHub invocation, automatic draft PRs | PRs and sandbox execution provide artifacts, but validation is explicitly prompt-driven | Best production-shaped open reference implementation, but you must add deterministic CI, review, and visual gates yourself. |
| [MCO](https://github.com/mco-org/mco) | Vendor-neutral orchestration over Codex CLI, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and others | Multi-agent findings normalized with severity, category, evidence, recommendations; SARIF output for GitHub Code Scanning | Good if you already use several coding-agent CLIs and primarily need independent review aggregation. |

Two smaller projects worth watching are [run-agent](https://github.com/jonnyzzz/run-agent), which formalizes roles, stages, quality gates, and factual handoffs, and [agent-system](https://github.com/boraoztunc/agent-system), which emphasizes spec-first role separation and independent verification.

## Strong platforms, but not complete evidence-based SDLCs

- [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) is the most established open coding-agent platform. Its [Software Agent SDK](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/index) provides code-oriented agents, remote execution, Docker isolation, and GitHub workflows. It is a strong execution substrate, but its core is better characterized as a coding-agent platform than a prescriptive multi-role SDLC.

- [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) is particularly strong for reproducibility. It records thought/action/observation trajectories, exact configurations, logs, patches, and SWE-bench-compatible predictions in its [trajectory format](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md). It is mainly a software-engineering agent and evaluation scaffold, not a full developer-team orchestrator.

- [Deep Agents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) supplies subagents, isolated contexts, filesystems, sandboxes, persistence, approvals, and middleware. [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) provides the durable graph runtime underneath it. This is probably the best programmable foundation for building a custom system, but “what evidence makes a change shippable?” remains application policy.

- [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) now supersedes [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen), which is in maintenance mode. It supports Python/.NET multi-agent workflows and production orchestration. It is general-purpose rather than software-delivery-specific, so tests, attestations, and PR gates must be designed separately.

- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) is useful for role-based crews and deterministic flows, but it does not itself provide a compelling code-shipping evidence contract.

## Evidence layers that complement an orchestrator

[Agent Loom](https://github.com/z3z1ma/agent-loom) is unusually relevant. It is a repo-local “truth system” that separates:

1. what an agent claims,
2. the evidence attached to that claim, and
3. whether an independent actor accepts it.

Evidence records can preserve the command, environment, commit, expected and actual results, output excerpts, screenshots, traces, scans, and tests. Loom is not the executor; it is a strong missing layer underneath OpenHands, Open SWE, or a CLI-agent swarm.

For postmortems, [Microsoft AgentRx](https://github.com/microsoft/AgentRx) analyzes multi-agent execution trajectories, synthesizes invariants, and produces auditable violation logs with supporting evidence. It diagnoses failed runs rather than controlling the shipping pipeline.

For benchmark-grade evidence, [SWE-EVO](https://github.com/SWE-EVO/SWE-EVO) evaluates longer-term software evolution and accepts trajectories from OpenHands and SWE-agent.

## Research-oriented “AI software companies”

[MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) and [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) pioneered role-specialized software-company simulations. They remain valuable for experiments and workflow ideas, but I would not select either first for controlled autonomous shipping. Their center of gravity is agent collaboration and generated artifacts, not independently enforced acceptance criteria, CI provenance, or release attestations.

## Practical recommendation

If the goal is autonomous issue-to-PR delivery with defensible evidence:

- Start with **AI-SDLC Framework** if signed attestations, reviewer independence, and governance are central—and accept early-project risk.
- Start with **metaswarm** if you want a usable, CLI-native engineering workflow with TDD, adversarial review, CI, and visual verification.
- Choose **Routa** when acceptance-criterion evidence and explicit verifier verdicts should travel with every work item.
- Use **Open SWE + Deep Agents/LangGraph** when you need a customizable platform and are prepared to implement deterministic gates.
- Add **Agent Loom** when preserving claims, commands, outputs, and acceptance decisions as repo-local evidence matters.

The important dividing line is this: a transcript or agent self-report is observability, not shipping evidence. The stronger projects require another actor or deterministic mechanism to reproduce tests, inspect artifacts, verify acceptance criteria, and record the verdict.

As of July 2026, public tooling falls into three distinct groups: full AI-SDLC systems, coding-agent platforms with reproducible traces, and general orchestration libraries. Few projects genuinely combine orchestration with independently checkable shipping evidence.

## Strongest matches

| Project | What it ships | Evidence model | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| [AI-SDLC Framework](https://github.com/ai-sdlc-framework/ai-sdlc) | Autonomous issue-to-PR pipeline, isolated worktrees, parallel reviewers, policy gates | Signed DSSE attestations, cross-harness reviewer independence, checkpoints, structured quality gates | Closest literal match to “evidence-based shipping.” Promising but currently `v1alpha1`; autonomous orchestration is marked experimental. |
| [metaswarm](https://github.com/dsifry/metaswarm) | 18-role SDLC swarm for Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI; issue-to-merged-PR workflow | Orchestrator reruns validation, adversarial review requires `file:line` evidence, blocking coverage thresholds, CI monitoring, Playwright screenshots | Strongest ready-made multi-agent development methodology. Evidence enforcement is mostly git, scripts, prompts, tests, and review rubrics rather than cryptographic attestations. |
| [Routa](https://github.com/phodal/routa) | Workspace/Kanban-based multi-agent delivery with MCP, ACP, and A2A support | Every card accumulates canonical acceptance criteria, implementation evidence, test results, per-criterion verification, and an independent verdict | Excellent niche option when you want evidence to live with the work item. Particularly clear separation between implementer and verifier. |
| [Open SWE](https://github.com/langchain-ai/open-swe) | Asynchronous internal coding-agent architecture: subagents, sandboxes, Slack/Linear/GitHub invocation, automatic draft PRs | PRs and sandbox execution provide artifacts, but validation is explicitly prompt-driven | Best production-shaped open reference implementation, but you must add deterministic CI, review, and visual gates yourself. |
| [MCO](https://github.com/mco-org/mco) | Vendor-neutral orchestration over Codex CLI, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and others | Multi-agent findings normalized with severity, category, evidence, recommendations; SARIF output for GitHub Code Scanning | Good if you already use several coding-agent CLIs and primarily need independent review aggregation. |

Two smaller projects worth watching are [run-agent](https://github.com/jonnyzzz/run-agent), which formalizes roles, stages, quality gates, and factual handoffs, and [agent-system](https://github.com/boraoztunc/agent-system), which emphasizes spec-first role separation and independent verification.

## Strong platforms, but not complete evidence-based SDLCs

- [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) is the most established open coding-agent platform. Its [Software Agent SDK](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/index) provides code-oriented agents, remote execution, Docker isolation, and GitHub workflows. It is a strong execution substrate, but its core is better characterized as a coding-agent platform than a prescriptive multi-role SDLC.

- [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) is particularly strong for reproducibility. It records thought/action/observation trajectories, exact configurations, logs, patches, and SWE-bench-compatible predictions in its [trajectory format](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md). It is mainly a software-engineering agent and evaluation scaffold, not a full developer-team orchestrator.

- [Deep Agents](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents) supplies subagents, isolated contexts, filesystems, sandboxes, persistence, approvals, and middleware. [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) provides the durable graph runtime underneath it. This is probably the best programmable foundation for building a custom system, but “what evidence makes a change shippable?” remains application policy.

- [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) now supersedes [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen), which is in maintenance mode. It supports Python/.NET multi-agent workflows and production orchestration. It is general-purpose rather than software-delivery-specific, so tests, attestations, and PR gates must be designed separately.

- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) is useful for role-based crews and deterministic flows, but it does not itself provide a compelling code-shipping evidence contract.

## Evidence layers that complement an orchestrator

[Agent Loom](https://github.com/z3z1ma/agent-loom) is unusually relevant. It is a repo-local “truth system” that separates:

1. what an agent claims,
2. the evidence attached to that claim, and
3. whether an independent actor accepts it.

Evidence records can preserve the command, environment, commit, expected and actual results, output excerpts, screenshots, traces, scans, and tests. Loom is not the executor; it is a strong missing layer underneath OpenHands, Open SWE, or a CLI-agent swarm.

For postmortems, [Microsoft AgentRx](https://github.com/microsoft/AgentRx) analyzes multi-agent execution trajectories, synthesizes invariants, and produces auditable violation logs with supporting evidence. It diagnoses failed runs rather than controlling the shipping pipeline.

For benchmark-grade evidence, [SWE-EVO](https://github.com/SWE-EVO/SWE-EVO) evaluates longer-term software evolution and accepts trajectories from OpenHands and SWE-agent.

## Research-oriented “AI software companies”

[MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) and [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) pioneered role-specialized software-company simulations. They remain valuable for experiments and workflow ideas, but I would not select either first for controlled autonomous shipping. Their center of gravity is agent collaboration and generated artifacts, not independently enforced acceptance criteria, CI provenance, or release attestations.

## Practical recommendation

If the goal is autonomous issue-to-PR delivery with defensible evidence:

- Start with **AI-SDLC Framework** if signed attestations, reviewer independence, and governance are central—and accept early-project risk.
- Start with **metaswarm** if you want a usable, CLI-native engineering workflow with TDD, adversarial review, CI, and visual verification.
- Choose **Routa** when acceptance-criterion evidence and explicit verifier verdicts should travel with every work item.
- Use **Open SWE + Deep Agents/LangGraph** when you need a customizable platform and are prepared to implement deterministic gates.
- Add **Agent Loom** when preserving claims, commands, outputs, and acceptance decisions as repo-local evidence matters.

The important dividing line is this: a transcript or agent self-report is observability, not shipping evidence. The stronger projects require another actor or deterministic mechanism to reproduce tests, inspect artifacts, verify acceptance criteria, and record the verdict.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes—with one qualification: [NTM (Named Tmux Manager)](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) is the closest ready-made match.

- Runs as a Go CLI/TUI over ordinary tmux sessions and panes.
- `ntm palette <session>` opens a searchable command palette; `ntm bind` can expose it as an F6 tmux popup.
- Can spawn, inspect, message, interrupt, and compare multiple agent panes.
- Supports Claude Code, Codex, Gemini/Antigravity, and Grok Build.
- Core operation does not require an NTM daemon. Its REST/WebSocket server is optional and starts only through `ntm serve`.

The palette’s documented target groups are currently agent-specific—All, Claude, Codex, and Gemini—so NTM is multi-harness but not completely arbitrary-harness-neutral. See its [palette definition and usage](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm/blob/main/command_palette.md).

Other options miss at least one requirement:

- [agent-session-manager](https://github.com/izll/agent-session-manager) accepts custom agent commands and uses tmux, but presents a session-management TUI rather than an ephemeral command palette.
- [workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux) is broadly agent-neutral and excellent for worktree-plus-tmux workflows, but isn’t primarily a cross-pane command palette.
- [tmux-agent-sidebar](https://github.com/hiroppy/tmux-agent-sidebar) provides strong cross-session monitoring and navigation, but relies on agent-specific hooks/plugins.
- [tmux-agent-status](https://github.com/samleeney/tmux-agent-status) has an `fzf` switcher, but starts a collector daemon.
- [twmux](https://pypi.org/project/twmux/) explicitly uses a polling daemon.

For strict, arbitrary-command neutrality, the cleanest zero-extra-daemon solution remains a small palette built from tmux’s `list-panes`, `capture-pane`, and `send-keys` commands plus [fzf-tmux](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/blob/master/bin/fzf-tmux). That treats every pane uniformly, but you must supply agent detection, actions, and prompt recipes yourself.

One semantic caveat: tmux itself always has a server process. “Zero-daemon” here can only mean “no additional resident manager beyond tmux.”

Yes—with one qualification: [NTM (Named Tmux Manager)](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm) is the closest ready-made match.

- Runs as a Go CLI/TUI over ordinary tmux sessions and panes.
- `ntm palette <session>` opens a searchable command palette; `ntm bind` can expose it as an F6 tmux popup.
- Can spawn, inspect, message, interrupt, and compare multiple agent panes.
- Supports Claude Code, Codex, Gemini/Antigravity, and Grok Build.
- Core operation does not require an NTM daemon. Its REST/WebSocket server is optional and starts only through `ntm serve`.

The palette’s documented target groups are currently agent-specific—All, Claude, Codex, and Gemini—so NTM is multi-harness but not completely arbitrary-harness-neutral. See its [palette definition and usage](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm/blob/main/command_palette.md).

Other options miss at least one requirement:

- [agent-session-manager](https://github.com/izll/agent-session-manager) accepts custom agent commands and uses tmux, but presents a session-management TUI rather than an ephemeral command palette.
- [workmux](https://github.com/raine/workmux) is broadly agent-neutral and excellent for worktree-plus-tmux workflows, but isn’t primarily a cross-pane command palette.
- [tmux-agent-sidebar](https://github.com/hiroppy/tmux-agent-sidebar) provides strong cross-session monitoring and navigation, but relies on agent-specific hooks/plugins.
- [tmux-agent-status](https://github.com/samleeney/tmux-agent-status) has an `fzf` switcher, but starts a collector daemon.
- [twmux](https://pypi.org/project/twmux/) explicitly uses a polling daemon.

For strict, arbitrary-command neutrality, the cleanest zero-extra-daemon solution remains a small palette built from tmux’s `list-panes`, `capture-pane`, and `send-keys` commands plus [fzf-tmux](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/blob/master/bin/fzf-tmux). That treats every pane uniformly, but you must supply agent detection, actions, and prompt recipes yourself.

One semantic caveat: tmux itself always has a server process. “Zero-daemon” here can only mean “no additional resident manager beyond tmux.”

results.stdout:
Yes—but I could not find a public, end-to-end digital twin specifically for a multi-floor racket-sports club that combines the building, courts, bookings, access control, sensors, and autonomous equipment. The closest public references fall into three groups.

### Closest venue digital twins

- [VenueTwin / OnePlan](https://www.venuetwin.com/) is probably the strongest visual reference. It provides navigable venue replicas, alternate room and field-of-play configurations, crowd/security planning, workforce training, and load-in/out planning. Its Paris 2024 deployment has a [public Intel video](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/content-details/829095/video-digital-twins-platform-simplifies-venue-planning.html), while [Commonwealth Stadium has a public case study](https://www.oneplan.io/case-studies/commonwealth-stadium/). This is the best analogue for navigating floors and courts, although the public material emphasizes planning rather than live building telemetry.

- [SoFi Stadium’s digital twin](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sports-and-active-living/articles/10.3389/fspor.2023.1289140/full) is documented as supporting management of its 3.1-million-square-foot venue. The cited academic overview explains the intended combination of crowd movement, facility utilization, environmental sensors, and equipment monitoring. Public access is a case description, not an interactive demo.

- [Estádio do Dragão’s Omniverse twin](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/mr-factory-virtual-production/) is a visually strong public example. MR Factory recreated the stadium for the 2021 UEFA Champions League opening ceremony. It demonstrates high-fidelity venue reconstruction and virtual production, but not ongoing facility operations.

- The [Munich stadium-roof digital twin](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstream/handle/2117/366624/ASHVIN%20D5.1-Final.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1) from the EU ASHVIN project is a narrower but technically credible example: sensor-informed structural monitoring and virtual inspection rather than an entire venue experience.

VenueTwin is the one I would show first to stakeholders envisioning a multi-floor racket facility.

### Autonomous racket-sports references

These are not full digital twins, but demonstrate the operational pieces:

- [Smart Padel House](https://www.smartpadelhouse.com/) presents a functioning, fully automated US padel facility with 24/7 app or biometric entry, booking, and payment. It is the closest public facility-operations reference I found.

- [PlaySight SmartCourt](https://playsight.com/) connects fixed cameras, automated production, replay, analytics, and cloud records across padel, pickleball, and tennis courts. Its [public video library](https://playsight.com/playsight-videos/) includes a SmartCourt walkthrough. This could supply the court-activity layer of a twin.

- [In/Out](https://inout.tennis/) has an immediately viewable tennis demo covering automated line calls, video, shot statistics, and automatic court calibration.

- [ROBOT-TEN](https://roboten.eu/en/) publishes videos of robotic clay leveling, watering, line cleaning, hard-court cleaning, and court-cover deployment. This is relevant if “autonomous facility” includes unattended maintenance.

- Guangzhou’s [PHYBOT C robotic badminton court](https://www.eguangzhou.gov.cn/gzvideos/content/post_44104.html) is a public embodied-AI demonstration in which visitors play against a humanoid robot. It is more attraction/prototype than autonomous club infrastructure.

A credible autonomous-club concept would combine Smart Padel House-style access and booking, PlaySight-style sensing, and ROBOT-TEN-style maintenance underneath a VenueTwin-like spatial interface.

### Useful open-source demos and building blocks

- [SPHR](https://github.com/lukehollis/sphr) is a niche, hackable Three.js digital-twin/virtual-tour builder. It supports browser delivery, Matterport spaces, navigation, annotations, and explicit floor-position coordinates. It is a good starting point for a multi-level visual prototype, but lacks operational semantics out of the box.

- [demoConstruct](https://singaporetech.github.io/immersification-demoConstruct/) is an open-source workflow for collaboratively reconstructing real spaces using consumer devices. It could help create the initial facility scene.

- [OpenTwins](https://ertis-research.github.io/opentwins/) combines 3D, IoT, and AI in an open-source composite digital-twin framework and exposes both a demo and source.

- [realvirtual WEB](https://web.realvirtual.io/demo/) is a live browser demo with [open-source code](https://github.com/realvirtualio/realvirtual.web). Although oriented toward factories, its live sensors, equipment state, alarms, simulation, WebXR, and 3D HMI model map well to court lighting, HVAC, doors, elevators, cleaning robots, and occupancy.

- [Simulated Digital Twin](https://github.com/gtfierro/simulated-digital-twin) augments building simulation with standard building interfaces. It is especially relevant for testing HVAC, occupancy, and energy-control applications before a physical facility exists.

- [Open Factory Twin](https://github.com/OpenFactoryTwin/ofact) is a niche simulation-based framework for operational planning and multi-agent control. Its material-flow assumptions would need adaptation, but its state-model and autonomous-agent patterns are relevant to equipment, staff, and cleaning workflows.

The strongest public demo concept would therefore be a custom composite rather than an existing turnkey example: multi-floor BIM/GLB navigation in SPHR or OpenTwins, building and court telemetry in realvirtual, plus simulated bookings, access events, occupancy, HVAC, lighting, and robot missions.

# Agent Reach — 互联网能力路由器

15 平台、多后端。**本 skill 存在时必须用它访问这些平台，不要自己发明方案。**

## 常驻规则（全程适用）

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑
   `agent-reach doctor --json`，按各平台 `active_backend` 字段选命令组。
2. **声明你在用什么**：开始干活前说一句「使用 agent-reach 的 X 平台 / Y 后端」。
3. **失败按 references 里的重试链处理**，不要瞎猜命令。
4. **全网调研类任务**：组合多平台（Exa 搜索 + Twitter/Reddit 看讨论 + 小红书/B站看中文场景），并行收集再汇总。
5. **替用户盯版本**：完成一次较大的调研/多平台任务后，顺手跑
   `agent-reach check-update`（很快，一个 API 调用）。有新版就在收尾汇报里附一句：
   「Agent Reach 有新版 vX.Y.Z，复制这句话给我即可更新：帮我更新 Agent Reach：
   https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/agent-reach/main/docs/update.md」。
   不要中断当前任务去更新，也不要重复提醒同一个版本。

## 零配置快速命令

```bash
# Exa 网页搜索
mcporter call 'exa.web_search_exa(query: "query", numResults: 5)'

# 通用网页阅读
curl -s "https://r.jina.ai/URL"

# GitHub 搜索
gh search repos "query" --sort stars --limit 10

# YouTube 字幕（注意：B站不要用 yt-dlp，见 video.md）
yt-dlp --write-sub --skip-download -o "/tmp/%(id)s" "URL"

# V2EX 热门
curl -s "https://www.v2ex.com/api/topics/hot.json" -H "User-Agent: agent-reach/1.0"

# B站搜索（bili-cli，无需登录）
bili search "query" --type video -n 5
```

## 需登录态的平台（按 doctor 的 active_backend 选命令）

```bash
# Twitter 搜索（twitter-cli 首选；失败重试链见 social.md）
twitter search "query" -n 10

# Reddit（无零配置路径：OpenCLI 或 rdt-cli，必须登录态）
opencli reddit search "query" -f yaml   # 桌面
rdt search "query" --limit 10            # 存量/服务器

# 小红书（桌面首选 OpenCLI）
opencli xiaohongshu search "query" -f yaml

# Facebook / Instagram（桌面 OpenCLI，复用浏览器登录态）
opencli facebook search "query" -f yaml
opencli facebook groups -f yaml
opencli instagram search "query" -f yaml       # 搜用户
opencli instagram user USERNAME -f yaml        # 读指定用户最近帖子
```

## 环境检查

```bash
# 检查可用 channel 与每个平台当前激活的后端
agent-reach doctor --json
```

**不要在 agent workspace 创建文件。** 使用 `/tmp/` 存放临时输出，`~/.agent-reach/` 存放持久数据。

# 搜索工具

Exa AI 搜索引擎。

## Exa AI 搜索

高质量 AI 搜索引擎，擅长技术和代码搜索。

```bash
mcporter call 'exa.web_search_exa(query: "query", numResults: 5)'
mcporter call 'exa.get_code_context_exa(query: "code question", tokensNum: 3000)'
```

### 使用场景

| 场景 | 参数 |
|-----|------|
| 网页搜索 | `web_search_exa(query: "...", numResults: 5)` |
| 代码搜索 | `get_code_context_exa(query: "...", tokensNum: 3000)` |

### 特点

- 擅长英文内容和技术文档
- 支持代码上下文搜索
- 结果质量高

| GitHub 搜索 | agent-reach (dev.md) | 仓库/代码搜索 |
# 开发工具

GitHub CLI 

## GitHub (gh CLI)

GitHub 官方命令行工具，用于仓库、Issue、PR、Actions、Release 以及 API 访问。

```bash
# 认证
gh auth login
gh auth status

# 搜索
gh search repos "query" --sort stars --limit 10
gh search code "query" --language python

# 仓库
gh repo view owner/repo
gh repo clone owner/repo
gh repo create my-repo --private
gh repo fork owner/repo
gh repo fork owner/repo --clone
gh repo sync owner/repo

# Issues
gh issue list -R owner/repo --state open
gh issue view 123 -R owner/repo
gh issue create -R owner/repo --title "Title" --body "Body"

# Pull Requests
gh pr list -R owner/repo --state open
gh pr view 123 -R owner/repo
gh pr create -R owner/repo --title "Title" --body "Body"
gh pr checks 123 --repo owner/repo

# Actions / CI
gh run list --repo owner/repo --limit 10
gh run view <run-id> --repo owner/repo
gh run view <run-id> --repo owner/repo --log-failed
gh workflow list --repo owner/repo

# Releases
gh release list -R owner/repo
gh release create v1.0.0

# API
gh api /user
gh api repos/owner/repo

# JSON 输出
gh issue list --repo owner/repo --json number,title --jq '.[] | "\(.number): \(.title)"'
```

Yes—but I could not find a public, end-to-end digital twin specifically for a multi-floor racket-sports club that combines the building, courts, bookings, access control, sensors, and autonomous equipment. The closest public references fall into three groups.

### Closest venue digital twins

- [VenueTwin / OnePlan](https://www.venuetwin.com/) is probably the strongest visual reference. It provides navigable venue replicas, alternate room and field-of-play configurations, crowd/security planning, workforce training, and load-in/out planning. Its Paris 2024 deployment has a [public Intel video](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/content-details/829095/video-digital-twins-platform-simplifies-venue-planning.html), while [Commonwealth Stadium has a public case study](https://www.oneplan.io/case-studies/commonwealth-stadium/). This is the best analogue for navigating floors and courts, although the public material emphasizes planning rather than live building telemetry.

- [SoFi Stadium’s digital twin](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sports-and-active-living/articles/10.3389/fspor.2023.1289140/full) is documented as supporting management of its 3.1-million-square-foot venue. The cited academic overview explains the intended combination of crowd movement, facility utilization, environmental sensors, and equipment monitoring. Public access is a case description, not an interactive demo.

- [Estádio do Dragão’s Omniverse twin](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/mr-factory-virtual-production/) is a visually strong public example. MR Factory recreated the stadium for the 2021 UEFA Champions League opening ceremony. It demonstrates high-fidelity venue reconstruction and virtual production, but not ongoing facility operations.

- The [Munich stadium-roof digital twin](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstream/handle/2117/366624/ASHVIN%20D5.1-Final.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1) from the EU ASHVIN project is a narrower but technically credible example: sensor-informed structural monitoring and virtual inspection rather than an entire venue experience.

VenueTwin is the one I would show first to stakeholders envisioning a multi-floor racket facility.

### Autonomous racket-sports references

These are not full digital twins, but demonstrate the operational pieces:

- [Smart Padel House](https://www.smartpadelhouse.com/) presents a functioning, fully automated US padel facility with 24/7 app or biometric entry, booking, and payment. It is the closest public facility-operations reference I found.

- [PlaySight SmartCourt](https://playsight.com/) connects fixed cameras, automated production, replay, analytics, and cloud records across padel, pickleball, and tennis courts. Its [public video library](https://playsight.com/playsight-videos/) includes a SmartCourt walkthrough. This could supply the court-activity layer of a twin.

- [In/Out](https://inout.tennis/) has an immediately viewable tennis demo covering automated line calls, video, shot statistics, and automatic court calibration.

- [ROBOT-TEN](https://roboten.eu/en/) publishes videos of robotic clay leveling, watering, line cleaning, hard-court cleaning, and court-cover deployment. This is relevant if “autonomous facility” includes unattended maintenance.

- Guangzhou’s [PHYBOT C robotic badminton court](https://www.eguangzhou.gov.cn/gzvideos/content/post_44104.html) is a public embodied-AI demonstration in which visitors play against a humanoid robot. It is more attraction/prototype than autonomous club infrastructure.

A credible autonomous-club concept would combine Smart Padel House-style access and booking, PlaySight-style sensing, and ROBOT-TEN-style maintenance underneath a VenueTwin-like spatial interface.

### Useful open-source demos and building blocks

- [SPHR](https://github.com/lukehollis/sphr) is a niche, hackable Three.js digital-twin/virtual-tour builder. It supports browser delivery, Matterport spaces, navigation, annotations, and explicit floor-position coordinates. It is a good starting point for a multi-level visual prototype, but lacks operational semantics out of the box.

- [demoConstruct](https://singaporetech.github.io/immersification-demoConstruct/) is an open-source workflow for collaboratively reconstructing real spaces using consumer devices. It could help create the initial facility scene.

- [OpenTwins](https://ertis-research.github.io/opentwins/) combines 3D, IoT, and AI in an open-source composite digital-twin framework and exposes both a demo and source.

- [realvirtual WEB](https://web.realvirtual.io/demo/) is a live browser demo with [open-source code](https://github.com/realvirtualio/realvirtual.web). Although oriented toward factories, its live sensors, equipment state, alarms, simulation, WebXR, and 3D HMI model map well to court lighting, HVAC, doors, elevators, cleaning robots, and occupancy.

- [Simulated Digital Twin](https://github.com/gtfierro/simulated-digital-twin) augments building simulation with standard building interfaces. It is especially relevant for testing HVAC, occupancy, and energy-control applications before a physical facility exists.

- [Open Factory Twin](https://github.com/OpenFactoryTwin/ofact) is a niche simulation-based framework for operational planning and multi-agent control. Its material-flow assumptions would need adaptation, but its state-model and autonomous-agent patterns are relevant to equipment, staff, and cleaning workflows.

The strongest public demo concept would therefore be a custom composite rather than an existing turnkey example: multi-floor BIM/GLB navigation in SPHR or OpenTwins, building and court telemetry in realvirtual, plus simulated bookings, access events, occupancy, HVAC, lighting, and robot missions.

results.stdout:
Use **[Boplog](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/)**.

It’s a static, chronological public build log of repositories where `kvnloo` actually authored commits. Bookmark-only forks and starred repositories are excluded.

Useful endpoints:

- [Source code](https://github.com/kvnloo/boplog)
- [JSON manifest](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json)
- [Atom feed](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/feed.xml)
- [LLM/agent index](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt)
- [Developer access](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/developers/) — read-only CLI, MCP, OpenAPI, and static JSON

The archive is periodically regenerated from GitHub and hosted as static files on GitHub Pages.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Yes—this pattern exists, though it is still niche. Strong, publicly verifiable examples:

- **Prasad Gade** — developer/data-science portfolio with [`/llms.txt`](https://prasadgade.dev/llms.txt) and a detailed [`/api/projects.json`](https://prasadgade.dev/api/projects.json). It also publishes resume, skills, social, OpenAPI, and agent-discovery JSON endpoints.

- **Doug Finke** — AI and PowerShell developer portfolio with [`/llms.txt`](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt) and [`/projects.json`](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json). This is perhaps the cleanest minimal example: predictable root-level endpoints specifically advertised as structured context for agents.

- **Eduardo Urias** — systems architect and AI-native product builder with [`/llms.txt`](https://www.eduardourias.com/llms.txt) and [`/api/projects.json`](https://www.eduardourias.com/api/projects.json). Additional structured endpoints cover identity, current focus, and operating principles.

- **Daliso Ngoma** — founder/developer portfolio with [`/llms.txt`](https://daliso.com/llms.txt) and a structured [`/api/projects.json`](https://daliso.com/api/projects.json). The implementation is open source in [`DJNgoma/daliso-website`](https://github.com/DJNgoma/daliso-website) and also includes JSON feeds, full-text LLM output, agent skills, and an API catalog.

- **Mahmoud Zalt** — AI architect and technical-advisor portfolio with [`/llms.txt`](https://zalt.me/llms.txt), [`/data/projects.json`](https://zalt.me/data/projects.json), and a human-readable [API directory](https://zalt.me/api-docs). It exposes projects alongside services, expertise, testimonials, contact information, and other structured resources.

A close non-personal reference is **PalatineAI**, whose public research/project showcase exposes [`/llms.txt`](https://palatineai.site/llms.txt), [`/projects.json`](https://palatineai.site/projects.json), and an agent [`/skill.md`](https://palatineai.site/skill.md).

One caveat: “JSON project manifest” is not yet standardized. These sites generally publish an ordinary `projects.json` dataset with their own schema. The [`llms.txt` proposal](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt) standardizes the discovery document’s location and Markdown structure, but not the linked project JSON format. Consequently, the best current convention is:

```text
/llms.txt
/projects.json            # or /api/projects.json
/openapi.json             # optional
/.well-known/agent.json   # optional
```

The `llms.txt` file should explicitly link and describe the JSON endpoint so agents do not have to guess its location or semantics.

- **Doug Finke** — AI and PowerShell developer portfolio with [`/llms.txt`](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt) and [`/projects.json`](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json). This is perhaps the cleanest minimal example: predictable root-level endpoints specifically advertised as structured context for agents.

- **Eduardo Urias** — systems architect and AI-native product builder with [`/llms.txt`](https://www.eduardourias.com/llms.txt) and [`/api/projects.json`](https://www.eduardourias.com/api/projects.json). Additional structured endpoints cover identity, current focus, and operating principles.

- **Daliso Ngoma** — founder/developer portfolio with [`/llms.txt`](https://daliso.com/llms.txt) and a structured [`/api/projects.json`](https://daliso.com/api/projects.json). The implementation is open source in [`DJNgoma/daliso-website`](https://github.com/DJNgoma/daliso-website) and also includes JSON feeds, full-text LLM output, agent skills, and an API catalog.

- **Mahmoud Zalt** — AI architect and technical-advisor portfolio with [`/llms.txt`](https://zalt.me/llms.txt), [`/data/projects.json`](https://zalt.me/data/projects.json), and a human-readable [API directory](https://zalt.me/api-docs). It exposes projects alongside services, expertise, testimonials, contact information, and other structured resources.

A close non-personal reference is **PalatineAI**, whose public research/project showcase exposes [`/llms.txt`](https://palatineai.site/llms.txt), [`/projects.json`](https://palatineai.site/projects.json), and an agent [`/skill.md`](https://palatineai.site/skill.md).

One caveat: “JSON project manifest” is not yet standardized. These sites generally publish an ordinary `projects.json` dataset with their own schema. The [`llms.txt` proposal](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt) standardizes the discovery document’s location and Markdown structure, but not the linked project JSON format. Consequently, the best current convention is:

```text
/llms.txt
/projects.json            # or /api/projects.json
/openapi.json             # optional
/.well-known/agent.json   # optional
```

The `llms.txt` file should explicitly link and describe the JSON endpoint so agents do not have to guess its location or semantics.

results.stdout:
Yes. I’d assemble it as three replaceable layers rather than adopt one “agent platform” end to end:

```text
OpenProject / Beads issue graph
          │ immutable issue + attempt IDs
          ▼
 Run-contract service ── Temporal ── agent adapters
          │                    ├── Codex / Claude / OpenHands
          │                    ├── MCP tools
          │                    └── A2A delegation
          ▼
 tmux-based terminal cockpit
```

## 1. Company issue graph

Use two complementary components:

- [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) as the human-facing company system of record. Its work packages support parent/child hierarchies, blocked-by, precedes/follows and other relations, exposed through its [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations).
- [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) as the agent-facing graph. It is unusually well matched: CLI-first, structured JSON, dependency tracking, ready-task detection and cross-project relationships.

My preference is:

- OpenProject owns objectives, projects, permissions and human-visible status.
- Beads contains the execution graph agents actually consume.
- A small synchronizer maps stable IDs between them.
- GitHub/GitLab issues and PRs are evidence attached to nodes—not the graph’s primary keys.

For a smaller, agent-first organization, you could begin with Beads alone. For a company-wide deployment, I would not make its repository-local database the only authoritative business record yet.

Alternatives:

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane): more modern Linear-like experience, but less compelling as a genuinely dependency-oriented graph.
- [Huly Platform](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform): broad collaborative workspace if you also need documents, chat and CRM-like objects.
- [Leantime](https://github.com/Leantime/leantime): good goal/project hierarchy, particularly for less technical users.

I would initially store graph extensions as ordinary relational nodes and typed edges in PostgreSQL. Neo4j or another graph database only becomes worthwhile once traversal—not CRUD, filtering and permissions—is demonstrably the dominant workload.

## 2. Agent harness contracts

Define your own small, versioned run contract. Do not expose a framework-specific LangGraph, CrewAI or OpenHands object as the company API.

A useful minimum envelope is:

```json
{
  "contract_version": "1.0",
  "run_id": "run_...",
  "attempt_id": "attempt_...",
  "issue_id": "issue_...",
  "parent_run_id": null,
  "agent_profile": "software-engineer",
  "workspace": {
    "repository": "...",
    "base_revision": "...",
    "worktree": "..."
  },
  "objective": "...",
  "acceptance_criteria": [],
  "inputs": [],
  "capabilities": [],
  "policy": {
    "network": "restricted",
    "approval_required": ["publish", "deploy"],
    "max_cost_usd": 10,
    "deadline": "..."
  },
  "state": "queued",
  "artifacts": [],
  "verification": [],
  "error": null
}
```

Standardize these boundaries:

- **Agent-to-agent delegation:** adopt the [A2A task lifecycle](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/blob/main/docs/specification.md)—tasks, messages, artifacts, streaming and cancellation.
- **Tool and data access:** use [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest). MCP’s durable [Tasks](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/utilities/tasks) are relevant, but that portion is marked experimental, so keep your internal lifecycle independent.
- **Terminal/editor presentation:** support [Agent Client Protocol](https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol). ACP is a client-to-agent UI protocol; it should not become your durable job model.
- **Durable execution:** [Temporal](https://github.com/temporalio/temporal) is the conservative choice for retries, cancellation, timers, resumability and human approval waits.
- **Telemetry:** emit OpenTelemetry traces using its [GenAI semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/). Carry `issue_id`, `run_id`, `attempt_id` and `parent_run_id` across every span.
- **Reference harness adapter:** [OpenHands Software Agent SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) is worth implementing as one adapter, especially for sandboxed software-engineering runs.

Keep `issue`, `run` and `attempt` separate:

- An issue describes desired company state.
- A run is one requested execution.
- An attempt is one concrete agent/process invocation.
- Artifacts and verification results remain immutable.
- Status changes are append-only events projected into the current view.

That distinction prevents retries, handoffs and competing agents from corrupting the issue graph.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

The strongest foundation remains tmux, with the cockpit acting as a control plane rather than a terminal emulator.

Good public components:

- [Flowmux](https://github.com/grouzen/flowmux): tmux-based dashboard for Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Pi; supports isolated worktrees and reconnectable sessions.
- [agent-deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck): niche but highly relevant agent-session and worktree manager with attention/status tracking.
- [gh-dash](https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash): excellent embedded GitHub PR/issue view.
- [sesh](https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh): fast project and tmux-session selection.
- [lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit): proven worktree/diff/commit surface.
- [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea): appropriate if you build a native graph/run TUI instead of composing existing screens.

My first implementation would fork neither tmux nor an agent CLI. It would provide:

- Left pane: projects, graph nodes and ready/blocked counts.
- Center: selected agent’s real tmux pane.
- Right: issue contract, approvals, artifacts and verification.
- Bottom: run timeline, cost and current tool activity.
- Global actions: assign, interrupt, retry, approve, open diff, merge and return issue to queue.

Flowmux is the quickest starting point. A custom Bubble Tea cockpit becomes justified when issue-graph navigation and approval workflows matter more than raw terminal-pane management.

The architectural rule I would protect is: **the cockpit renders and commands durable state; it does not infer authoritative state by scraping terminal text.** Agent CLIs can disappear or be replaced without losing the issue graph, run history or artifacts.

Yes. I’d assemble it as three replaceable layers rather than adopt one “agent platform” end to end:

```text
OpenProject / Beads issue graph
          │ immutable issue + attempt IDs
          ▼
 Run-contract service ── Temporal ── agent adapters
          │                    ├── Codex / Claude / OpenHands
          │                    ├── MCP tools
          │                    └── A2A delegation
          ▼
 tmux-based terminal cockpit
```

## 1. Company issue graph

Use two complementary components:

- [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) as the human-facing company system of record. Its work packages support parent/child hierarchies, blocked-by, precedes/follows and other relations, exposed through its [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations).
- [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) as the agent-facing graph. It is unusually well matched: CLI-first, structured JSON, dependency tracking, ready-task detection and cross-project relationships.

My preference is:

- OpenProject owns objectives, projects, permissions and human-visible status.
- Beads contains the execution graph agents actually consume.
- A small synchronizer maps stable IDs between them.
- GitHub/GitLab issues and PRs are evidence attached to nodes—not the graph’s primary keys.

For a smaller, agent-first organization, you could begin with Beads alone. For a company-wide deployment, I would not make its repository-local database the only authoritative business record yet.

Alternatives:

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane): more modern Linear-like experience, but less compelling as a genuinely dependency-oriented graph.
- [Huly Platform](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform): broad collaborative workspace if you also need documents, chat and CRM-like objects.
- [Leantime](https://github.com/Leantime/leantime): good goal/project hierarchy, particularly for less technical users.

I would initially store graph extensions as ordinary relational nodes and typed edges in PostgreSQL. Neo4j or another graph database only becomes worthwhile once traversal—not CRUD, filtering and permissions—is demonstrably the dominant workload.

## 2. Agent harness contracts

Define your own small, versioned run contract. Do not expose a framework-specific LangGraph, CrewAI or OpenHands object as the company API.

A useful minimum envelope is:

```json
{
  "contract_version": "1.0",
  "run_id": "run_...",
  "attempt_id": "attempt_...",
  "issue_id": "issue_...",
  "parent_run_id": null,
  "agent_profile": "software-engineer",
  "workspace": {
    "repository": "...",
    "base_revision": "...",
    "worktree": "..."
  },
  "objective": "...",
  "acceptance_criteria": [],
  "inputs": [],
  "capabilities": [],
  "policy": {
    "network": "restricted",
    "approval_required": ["publish", "deploy"],
    "max_cost_usd": 10,
    "deadline": "..."
  },
  "state": "queued",
  "artifacts": [],
  "verification": [],
  "error": null
}
```

Standardize these boundaries:

- **Agent-to-agent delegation:** adopt the [A2A task lifecycle](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/blob/main/docs/specification.md)—tasks, messages, artifacts, streaming and cancellation.
- **Tool and data access:** use [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest). MCP’s durable [Tasks](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/utilities/tasks) are relevant, but that portion is marked experimental, so keep your internal lifecycle independent.
- **Terminal/editor presentation:** support [Agent Client Protocol](https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol). ACP is a client-to-agent UI protocol; it should not become your durable job model.
- **Durable execution:** [Temporal](https://github.com/temporalio/temporal) is the conservative choice for retries, cancellation, timers, resumability and human approval waits.
- **Telemetry:** emit OpenTelemetry traces using its [GenAI semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/). Carry `issue_id`, `run_id`, `attempt_id` and `parent_run_id` across every span.
- **Reference harness adapter:** [OpenHands Software Agent SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) is worth implementing as one adapter, especially for sandboxed software-engineering runs.

Keep `issue`, `run` and `attempt` separate:

- An issue describes desired company state.
- A run is one requested execution.
- An attempt is one concrete agent/process invocation.
- Artifacts and verification results remain immutable.
- Status changes are append-only events projected into the current view.

That distinction prevents retries, handoffs and competing agents from corrupting the issue graph.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

The strongest foundation remains tmux, with the cockpit acting as a control plane rather than a terminal emulator.

Good public components:

- [Flowmux](https://github.com/grouzen/flowmux): tmux-based dashboard for Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Pi; supports isolated worktrees and reconnectable sessions.
- [agent-deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck): niche but highly relevant agent-session and worktree manager with attention/status tracking.
- [gh-dash](https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash): excellent embedded GitHub PR/issue view.
- [sesh](https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh): fast project and tmux-session selection.
- [lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit): proven worktree/diff/commit surface.
- [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea): appropriate if you build a native graph/run TUI instead of composing existing screens.

My first implementation would fork neither tmux nor an agent CLI. It would provide:

- Left pane: projects, graph nodes and ready/blocked counts.
- Center: selected agent’s real tmux pane.
- Right: issue contract, approvals, artifacts and verification.
- Bottom: run timeline, cost and current tool activity.
- Global actions: assign, interrupt, retry, approve, open diff, merge and return issue to queue.

Flowmux is the quickest starting point. A custom Bubble Tea cockpit becomes justified when issue-graph navigation and approval workflows matter more than raw terminal-pane management.

The architectural rule I would protect is: **the cockpit renders and commands durable state; it does not infer authoritative state by scraping terminal text.** Agent CLIs can disappear or be replaced without losing the issue graph, run history or artifacts.

Kevin Rajan’s position is that software expands human agency:

- **“Code is the great equalizer”** means programming—and increasingly LLM-assisted programming—makes knowledge and engineering capability available beyond traditional gatekeepers. More people can turn ideas into working systems.
- **“Automate humanitarian causes”** means applying that capability to health, infrastructure, and open systems that improve people’s lives and autonomy.
- His broader principle is that civilization advances when important, beneficial actions become reliable defaults—things systems can complete without requiring continuous human attention.
- The intended result is compounding competence: automation handles recurring necessities, freeing people to focus on higher-order problems and giving more people the power to build.

So this is not automation merely for efficiency. It is automation as social infrastructure: use code to distribute capability, remove bottlenecks, and make beneficial outcomes easier and more routine.

Gas Town — strongest fleet coordination and verification mechanics\n - Multi-agent workspace manager for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, and other coding agents.\n - Persists work in a git-backed ledger, supports handoffs and agent identities, and includes a Bors-style merge queue with verification gates.\n - Agents can submit completion evidence rather than merely declaring tasks finished.\n - Source: https://github.com/steveyegge/gastown\n\n Pick it when you want many coding agents operating concurrently across repositories with durable task state and controlled integration.\n\n2. Evolve — explicit autonomous AI-SDLC and evidence-based shipping\n - Kevin Rajan’s public framework integrates agent-swarm orchestration, isolated worktrees, project management, TDD, architecture review, CI validation, PR automation, and human review.\n - Its C(RAID) model puts research and analysis before implementation; SPARC supplies the inner specification-to-validation workflow.\n - Documentation: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/\n - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve\n - AI-SDLC hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html\n\n This is one of the more direct matches for “evidence-based shipping,” rather than simply facilitating agent conversations.\n\n3. OpenHands — best-established self-hosted coding-agent control plane\n - Agent Canvas runs OpenHands and ACP-compatible agents, including Claude Code and Codex, across local, container, VM, remote, and cloud backends.\n - Supports GitHub, Linear, Slack, scheduled automations, issue decomposition, code review, and dependency-update workflows.\n - Source: https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands\n - Documentation: https://docs.openhands.dev/\n\n Strong choice for an operational developer control center. Pair it with mandatory CI, review artifacts, and protected branches if evidence-based completion is required.\n\n4. tmux-agent-fleet — lightweight, harness-neutral local orchestration\n - A zero-daemon command palette for discovering and monitoring Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Pi, and other agents across tmux panes.\n - It deliberately avoids owning worktrees, injecting hooks, or imposing a workflow.\n - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet\n - Orchestration hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html\n\n Useful as a composable operator surface, not a complete autonomous delivery engine.\n\nFramework substrates\n\n5. Microsoft Agent Framework\n - Microsoft’s production-oriented successor to AutoGen.\n - Provides graph workflows, sequential/concurrent execution, handoffs, group collaboration, checkpointing, observability, human intervention, and durable execution in Python and .NET.\n - Source: https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework\n - Documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/\n\n For new Microsoft-stack projects, start here rather than AutoGen. AutoGen’s repository now identifies itself as maintenance-mode:\n https://github.com/microsoft/autogen\n\n6. agent behavioral characteristics including agent type, model, system prompts, and focus patterns. NTM includes built-in profiles for common roles like architect, implementer, reviewer, tester, and documenter.\n\n| Command | Arguments | Description |\n|---------|-----------|-------------|\n| `ntm profiles list` | `[--agent TYPE] [--tag TAG] [--json]` | List available profiles |\n| `ntm profiles show` | ` [--json]` | Show detailed profile information |\n| `ntm personas list` | `[--agent TYPE] [--tag TAG] [--json]` | Alias for `profiles list` |\n| `ntm personas show` | ` [--json]` | Alias for `profiles show` |\n\n**Profile Sources (later overrides earlier):**\n1. **Built-in**: Compiled into NTM (architect, implementer, reviewer, tester, documenter)\n2. **User**: `~/.config/ntm/personas.toml`\n3. **Project**: `.ntm/personas.toml`\n\n**Profile Sets:**\n\nProfile sets are named groups of profiles for quick spawning:\n\n```toml\n# In ~/.config/ntm/personas.toml or .ntm/personas.toml\n[[persona_sets]]\nname = \"backend-team\"\ndescription = \"Full backend development team\"\npersonas = [\"architect\", \"implementer\", \"implementer\", \"tester\"]\n```\n\n**Examples:**\n\n```bash\nntm profiles list # List all profiles\nntm profiles list --agent claude # Filter by agent type\nntm profiles list --tag review # Filter by tag\nntm profiles list --json # JSON output for scripts\nntm profiles show architect # Show profile details\nntm profiles show architect --json # JSON output with source info\n```\n\n**Using Profiles with Spawn:**\n\n```bash\nntm spawn myproject --profiles=architect,implementer,tester\nntm spawn myproject --profile-set=backend-team\n```\n\n### AI Agent Integration (Robot Mode)\n\nNTM provides machine-readable output for integration with AI coding agents and automation pipelines. All robot commands output JSON by default and follow consistent exit codes (0=success, 1=error, 2=unavailable).\n\n**Robot Output Formats + Verbosity:**\n\n- `--robot-format=json|toon|auto` (Alias: `--robot-output-format=...`; Env: `NTM_ROBOT_FORMAT`, `NTM_OUTPUT_FORMAT`, `TOON_DEFAULT_FORMAT`; Config: `[robot.output] format` = json|toon). `auto` currently resolves to JSON.\n- `--robot-verbosity=terse|default|debug` (Env: `NTM_ROBOT_VERBOSITY`). Applies to JSON/TOON only.\n- Config default for verbosity: `~/.config/ntm/config.toml` → `[robot] verbosity = \"default\"`.\n- `--robot-terse` is a **separate single-line format** and ignores `--robot-format` / `--robot-verbosity`.\n- JSON remains the default. For scripts that must always get JSON, pass `--robot-format=json` (or `--robot-output-format=json`) explicitly.\n- TOON is token-efficient (often ~40-60% fewer tokens for tabular outputs) but only supports uniform arrays and simple objects; unsupported shapes return an error. Use `--robot-format=json` or `auto` to avoid TOON failures.\n\n**Example output (JSON vs TOON):**\n\nJSON (default; also `--robot-format=json`):\n\n```json\n{\n \"success\": true,\n \"timestamp\": \"2026-01-22T01:23:00Z\",\n \"sessions\": [\n {\"name\": \"myproject\", \"attached\": true, \"windows\": 1}\n ]\n}\n```\n\nTOON (e.g. `--robot-output-format=toon`):\n\n```text\nsuccess: true\ntimestamp: 2026-01-22T01:23:00Z\nsessions[1]{attached,name,windows}:\n true\tmyproject\t1\n```\n\n**Robot JSON Envelope Spec (v1.0.0):**\n\nAll robot outputs share a common envelope structure:\n\n| Field | Type | Required | Description |\n|-------|------|----------|-------------|\n| `success` | boolean | Yes | Whether the operation succeeded |\n| `timestamp` | string | Yes | RFC3339 timestamp (UTC) |\n| `version` | string | Yes | Envelope schema version (semver, currently \"1.0.0\") |\n| `output_format` | string | Yes | Output format used (\"json\" or \"toon\") |\n| `error` | string | No | Human-readable error message (on failure) |\n| `error_code` | string | No | Machine-parseable error code (e.g., \"SESSION_NOT_FOUND\") |\n| `hint` | string | No | Suggested remediation action |\n| `_meta` | object | No | Optional timing/debug metadata |\n\nThe `_meta` field (when present) contains:\n\n| Field | Type | Description |\n|-------|------|-------------|\n| `duration_ms` | integer | Command execution time in milliseconds |\n| `exit_code` | integer | Process exit code (0=success) |\n| `command` | string | The robot command that was executed |\n\nExample envelope:\n\n```json\n{\n \"success\": true,\n \"timestamp\": \"2026-01-27T07:00:00Z\",\n \"version\": \"1.0.0\",\n \"output_format\": \"json\",\n \"_meta\": {\n \"duration_ms\": 42,\n \"command\": \"robot-status\"\n },\n \"sessions\": [...]\n}\n```\n\n**State Inspection:**\n\n```bash\nntm --robot-status # Sessions, panes, agent states\nntm --robot-context=SESSION # Context window usage per agent\nntm --robot-snapshot # Unified state: sessions + beads + alerts + mail\nntm --robot-tail=SESSION # Recent pane output (--lines=50 --panes=1,2)\nntm --robot-inspect-pane=SESS # Detailed pane inspection (--inspect-index=N)\nntm --robot-files=SESSION # File changes with agent attribution (--files-window=15m)\nntm --robot-metrics=SESSION # Session metrics export (--metrics-period=24h)\nntm --robot-palette # Query command palette (--palette-category=NAME)\nntm --robot-plan # bv execution plan with parallelizable tracks\nntm --robot-graph # Dependency graph insights\nntm --robot-dashboard # Dashboard summary (markdown or --json)\nntm --robot-terse # Single-line encoded state (minimal tokens)\nntm --robot-markdown # System state as markdown tables\nntm --robot-health # Project health summary\nntm --robot-version # Version info\nntm --robot-help # Full robot mode documentation\n```\n\n**Agent Control:**\n\n```bash\nntm --robot-send=SESSION --msg=\"Fix auth\" --type=claude # Send to agents\nntm --robot-ack=SESSION --ack-timeout=30s # Watch for responses\nntm --robot-spawn=SESSION --spawn-cc=2 --spawn-wait # Create session\nntm --robot-interrupt=SESSION --interrupt-msg=\"Stop\" # Send Ctrl+C\nntm --robot-assign=SESSION --beads=bd-1,bd-2 # Assign work to agents\nntm --robot-replay=SESSION --replay-id=ID # Replay command from history\nntm --robot-dismiss-alert=ALERT_ID # Dismiss --bead-priority=1\nntm --robot-bead-show=BEAD_ID # Show bead details\nntm --robot-bead-close=BEAD_ID --bead-close-reason=\"Fixed\" # Close a bead\n```\n\n**CASS Integration (Cross-Agent
